title: Part 3 — JavaScript
tagline: Syntax, the DOM, calling APIs, and three projects of your own before React.
intro: The most important part of the path: React is JavaScript and so is Node. Learn it well here and the next two parts get half as hard.
Every section has runnable code: copy it into a file, run it, then change one detail and see what differs.

blocks.caption: From the first line of code to a page that calls an API.

items.label: Where JavaScript runs
items.detail: The browser console, a .js file in HTML, or node in a terminal
explain: The console (F12 → Console) runs a line at once, good for trying things. A .js file loaded by a script tag is for real pages.
node app.js runs the same language outside the browser: no document or window, but files and the network. Part 5 works this way.

items.label: The basics
explain: const for values never reassigned, let when you must; never var. Compare with === to avoid hidden conversion: 1 == '1' is true, 1 === '1' is false.
Template strings join text more neatly: `Hello ${name}` instead of 'Hello ' + name.

items.label: Arrays, objects, functions
items.detail: Data as lists and records, transformed with map, filter, reduce
explain: An object groups facts about one thing: { name: 'Shirt', price: 150000 }. An array holds many: a product list.
map transforms each item, filter keeps matching ones, reduce folds the array into one value, such as a cart total.
A callback is a function handed to another to call later. map, filter and addEventListener all take one.

items.label: The DOM & events
items.detail: Find elements on the page, change them, respond to clicks and submits
explain: The DOM is the tree the browser builds from HTML. document.querySelector('.todo-list') fetches an element; element.textContent changes its text.
addEventListener('click', handler) runs handler on every click. On a form, call event.preventDefault() so submitting does not reload the page.

items.label: Async: Promises, fetch
items.detail: Call APIs without freezing the page while waiting
explain: fetch returns a Promise: a result that arrives later. await waits for it inside an async function, so the code reads top to bottom as usual.
Always check response.ok: fetch does not throw on a 404 or 500 from the server, only when the network fails.
JSON is the format APIs answer in. response.json() turns a JSON string into a JavaScript object.

items.label: Advanced: scope, closures, this
items.detail: What explains code behaving differently from what you expected
explain: Scope decides where a variable is visible. A closure is a function that remembers the variables where it was made, even after that code has finished.
this depends on how a function is called, not where it is written. Arrow functions have no this of their own, which suits callbacks.

sections.title: Where to run JavaScript
sections.summary: Three places, all used in this part.

items: Quick tries: open any page, press F12, pick the Console tab, type 2 + 3 and press Enter.
On your own page: create app.js next to index.html and load it with a deferred script tag, so it runs after the HTML is built.
In a terminal: node app.js runs a file without a browser. Use it for pure logic exercises such as sums or filtering.

sections.title: Promises, async/await and fetch
sections.summary: How to call an API; React and Node do it exactly this way.

items: A Promise is a result that comes later: success (resolve) or failure (reject).
async before a function allows await inside it; await pauses that function until the Promise settles, while the page keeps running.
try/catch catches await's errors: no network, broken JSON, or the error you throw when response.ok is false.
localStorage stores strings in the browser: JSON.stringify before saving, JSON.parse when reading back.
